items.title: How Vienna keeps rents low
items.passage: About half of the people in Vienna live in housing that the city built or subsidised. The city started building in the 1920s and never stopped. It owns about 220,000 flats and supports many more built by nonprofit associations.
items.text:
About half of the people in Vienna live in housing that the city built or subsidised. The city started building in the 1920s and never stopped. It owns about 220,000 flats and supports many more built by nonprofit associations.

Rents in these flats are set to cover costs, not to make a profit. Income limits apply when you move in, but not afterwards, so the buildings house a mix of incomes.

The city also buys land early, before prices rise, and runs design competitions for new projects. The result is a large stock of good, ordinary housing that keeps private rents in check too.

items.title: Why batteries now undercut gas peaker plants
items.passage: Battery storage now wins auctions for peak capacity that gas plants used to win. Four years of auction results show the price per kilowatt of battery capacity falling by more than half, while gas turbine prices rose with demand for new turbines.
items.text:
Battery storage now wins auctions for peak capacity that gas plants used to win. Four years of auction results show the price per kilowatt of battery capacity falling by more than half, while gas turbine prices rose with demand for new turbines.

Peaker plants run only a few hundred hours a year, when demand is highest. That makes them a good match for batteries, which charge when power is cheap and discharge for two to four hours in the evening.

The batteries do not replace every gas plant. Long cold spells with little wind still need firm power for days, not hours. But for the daily evening peak, the numbers have changed, and grid operators are changing their plans to match.

items.author: Abyss Notes
items.passage: Mussel beds, tube worms and a very curious octopus.
items.transcript:
We are at about 1,200 metres on the edge of a cold seep. On the left you can see the mussel bed. The mussels have bacteria in their gills that live on methane coming out of the seafloor.

The white patches are bacterial mats. Further up there are tube worms, and here is an octopus that has been following the vehicle for ten minutes.

We take a push core here, a short tube of sediment, to look at the microbes back in the lab.

items.title: Hydrothermal vent
items.passage: Hydrothermal vents are places where seawater seeps into the crust, heats up near magma and comes back out loaded with minerals. The water can be hotter than 350 C and does not boil because of the pressure.
items.text:
Hydrothermal vents are places where seawater seeps into the crust, heats up near magma and comes back out loaded with minerals. The water can be hotter than 350 C and does not boil because of the pressure.

Around the vents live animals that do not depend on sunlight. Bacteria use the chemical energy in hydrogen sulfide to make food, and tube worms, clams and shrimp live off those bacteria, some of them with the bacteria inside their own bodies.

The first vents were found in 1977 near the Galapagos Islands. Since then researchers have found hundreds, on every ocean ridge they have searched.

items.title: Miso in 90 days, start to finish
items.author: Crock and Jar
items.passage: Soybeans, koji and salt in a crock, opened once a month on camera.
items.transcript:
This is day one. Soybeans soaked overnight, cooked until you can crush one between two fingers. We mash them, mix in the koji and the salt, and pack it into the crock with no air pockets.

Day thirty. We open it, and there is a little mould on top, which is normal. Scrape it off. The paste underneath smells sweet and a bit like soy sauce.

Day ninety. The color is light brown and the taste is salty, sweet and deep. This is a young white miso. You can leave it for a year if you want it darker and stronger.

items.title: A beginner's guide to koji at home
items.passage: Koji is rice or barley with a mould called Aspergillus oryzae growing on it. The mould makes enzymes that break starch into sugar and protein into amino acids, and that is where the sweetness of miso and the depth of soy sauce come from.
items.text:
Koji is rice or barley with a mould called Aspergillus oryzae growing on it. The mould makes enzymes that break starch into sugar and protein into amino acids, and that is where the sweetness of miso and the depth of soy sauce come from.

You need steamed rice, koji spores, a clean cloth and somewhere that stays at about 30 C for two days. A cooler box with a heating pad and a cheap thermometer is enough. Spread the rice in a thin layer, dust it with spores, cover it and wait.

After about 18 hours the rice smells like chestnuts and you can see a white fuzz. Break up the clumps so air gets in. By 40 to 48 hours the grains should be covered in white. If you see green or yellow, it went too far and started to make spores.

Use the koji fresh, dry it, or freeze it. Shio koji, a mix of koji, salt and water, is the easiest place to start.

items.title: Servo or stepper for a robot arm?
items.author: Bench Robotics Lab
items.passage: Side by side tests on a cheap arm, with a kitchen scale to measure torque.
items.transcript:
Today we are testing a servo and a stepper on the same arm. The arm is cheap, printed, and the payload is a kitchen scale so we can read the force.

First the servo. It is quick and it holds position well, but when we push past about 400 grams the gears start to buzz and it drifts.

Now the stepper with a small gearbox. Slower to move, but it holds 900 grams without complaint. The catch is that it does not know where it is if it skips a step, so we add an end stop.

My pick for a desk arm: steppers on the shoulder and elbow, a servo on the gripper.

items.title: I tried five note apps in a year. This is what stuck.
items.passage: What stuck: plain text files in folders, with dates in the file names. Every app could open them, every search tool could index them, and moving them took seconds.
items.text:
I used five note apps in twelve months, each for at least two months. I moved my notes every time, which taught me more than the apps did.

What stuck: plain text files in folders, with dates in the file names. Every app could open them, every search tool could index them, and moving them took seconds.

What did not stick: tags. I tagged with care for three weeks and then stopped. Search found everything the tags would have found.

The one feature I miss from the fancier apps is backlinks. I solved that with a search for the file name.

items.title: Subtractive synthesis on one page
items.passage: Subtractive synthesis starts with a bright, harmonically rich wave from an oscillator, usually a sawtooth or a square. A filter then removes part of the sound, most often the high frequencies. An amplifier controlled by an envelope shapes how loud the sound is over time.
items.text:
Subtractive synthesis starts with a bright, harmonically rich wave from an oscillator, usually a sawtooth or a square. A filter then removes part of the sound, most often the high frequencies. An amplifier controlled by an envelope shapes how loud the sound is over time.

That is the whole chain: oscillator, filter, amplifier, envelope. Most classic synthesizer sounds come from changing just two things, the filter cutoff and the envelope's attack and decay.

Start with one oscillator and the filter fully open. Close the filter slowly while a note plays and listen to the sound get darker. Then give the filter its own envelope and you have the sound of most bass lines from the 1980s.

items.title: Designing a variable font: notes from my first year
items.passage: A variable font holds a whole range of styles in one file. You draw a few masters, for example a thin and a black weight, and the font interpolates everything in between.
items.text:
A variable font holds a whole range of styles in one file. You draw a few masters, for example a thin and a black weight, and the font interpolates everything in between.

The hard part is keeping the masters compatible. Every glyph needs the same number of points, in the same order, in every master. One extra point in the bold g and the interpolation breaks, and you only notice it at weight 512.

My first year taught me to draw the extremes first, test the middle often, and keep the number of axes small. Weight and optical size cover most needs. Every extra axis multiplies the work.

items.title: How one city doubled bike trips in five years
items.passage: The city did something unusual: it built a connected network of protected lanes before it argued about each street. In the first year, the council drew a map of 80 kilometres of routes that joined schools, stations and the centre, and built most of it with temporary kerbs and planters.
items.text:
The city did something unusual: it built a connected network of protected lanes before it argued about each street. In the first year, the council drew a map of 80 kilometres of routes that joined schools, stations and the centre, and built most of it with temporary kerbs and planters.

Bike trips doubled in five years. The biggest increase was in short trips under three kilometres, many of them by women and children, who had not ridden much before.

Shop owners worried about parking. A survey two years later found that most of their customers had arrived on foot, by bike or by tram all along. The temporary kerbs are now being replaced with permanent ones.
